title: Scottish shortbread
summary: A buttery almond-flour shortbread round, scored into petticoat-tail wedges and baked low until sandy and pale.
steps: Heat the oven to 150 °C (300 °F). Line the base of a 20 cm (8 in) round tin with parchment.
Beat the butter, powdered erythritol, vanilla and salt until smooth. Stir in the almond flour and coconut flour to a soft dough; don't overwork it.
Press evenly into the tin. Crimp the edge with your fingers, score into 12 wedges and prick all over with a fork.
Chill 30 minutes so the butter firms and the shortbread keeps its sandy texture.
Bake 28–32 minutes, until firm and pale golden at the edges. Sprinkle with the erythritol and re-cut along the scores while warm.
Cool completely in the tin before lifting out; it is crumbly until cold.
dairy_free_notes: Shortbread is mostly butter, so the dairy-free version tastes noticeably different; choose a dairy-free butter you like on its own, and add a pinch more salt.
tips: Low heat is the point: shortbread should be pale, not browned.

origin.history: Shortbread grew out of medieval 'biscuit bread', twice-baked dough that bakers enriched with butter in place of yeast. By the sixteenth century it was a Scottish luxury for festivals such as Hogmanay. The story that Mary, Queen of Scots, favoured the thin wedges called petticoat tails is popular but unproven.
